analysis.one_liner: Extends brand-name drug monopolies from three to five years for reformulated and re-approved drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Energy and Commerce Committee after its March 2015 referral, dying without a vote by the end of the 114th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, a company that wins FDA approval for a new use, reformulation, or redesign of an already-approved drug gets three years of exclusive marketing before copies can compete. This bill would stretch that exclusivity to five years, in both the brand-name and generic drug approval pathways, when the company shows the change helps patients stick to treatment, reduces risks or side effects, or offers other comparable benefits. It also would have required HHS to write rules, including a consultation process with the drug companies claiming the extension, within 180 days. Longer exclusivity means a longer window in which no cheaper generic version of the same active ingredient can reach the market for those uses.
analysis.who_benefits: Brand-name drug makers that reformulate existing drugs or win approval for new uses. They would keep exclusive rights for five years instead of three, adding two years of monopoly pricing on drugs they did not originally invent.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds 24 months to the three-year marketing exclusivity period for certain new drug applications, for a total of five years [S2].

The extension applies when a drug wins approval for a new indication or use, or is reformulated or redesigned in ways that promote patient adherence, reduce public health risks, cut side effects, benefit the health-care system, or provide other comparable patient benefits [S2].
The same extension is written into the abbreviated new drug application pathway, so it reaches the approval route for generic-style applications too [S3].

Within 180 days of enactment, the HHS Secretary would have to issue final regulations, including a process for consulting with companies claiming the extension about whether their drug provides the required benefit [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Patients, employers, and government health programs that buy those drugs. Every extra year of exclusivity delays cheaper generic competition, so users of the affected drugs pay brand-name prices for longer.
analysis.who_pays_short: Patients and health plans buying the drugs

drawbacks.text: The extension covers drugs whose active ingredient was already FDA-approved, meaning two additional monopoly years on products that are not genuinely new medicines, which delays the lower prices generics bring [S2].

The qualifying criteria are open-ended: a company can qualify for 'other patient benefits that are comparable,' and the standard is determined in consultation with the company making the claim, giving manufacturers significant say in whether they qualify [S3].

Reformulations are a well-known strategy for extending patent life on old drugs, so critics of the current three-year exclusivity argue this bill would reward that practice with two more years of it (general knowledge about how reformulation extends exclusivity).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is framed as rewarding patient-centered innovation, and encouraging companies to make drugs easier to take or safer has some real value. But the cost falls directly on people who need the drugs: two more years without generic competition on medicines whose core ingredient is already approved. The loose 'comparable benefits' standard and the consultation with the manufacturer itself make it easy for companies to claim the extension. On balance, the bill trades higher drug prices for patients and health programs in exchange for a modest incentive to tweak existing drugs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Gus Bilirakis introduced the bill on March 13, 2015, joined by Representatives Connolly, Israel, and Griffith as original cosponsors [S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and a week later to the subcommittee handling health matters [S5].
The committee took no further action; the bill's action history ends with the subcommittee referral, and it never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because it died, drug prices on reformulated medicines were not extended by two extra monopoly years, so patients, health plans, and generic drug makers are better off than they would have been had it passed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Patients, payers, and generic drug makers

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican and the four cosponsors split evenly between two Republicans and two Democrats; the bill's failure reflected committee inaction, not a party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill would have added two years of exclusive marketing on reformulated and newly indicated versions of already-approved drugs, letting companies charge brand-name prices longer. That gain comes directly out of patients' and health programs' pockets.
Every added exclusivity year postpones the day a generic version can be sold for the affected uses, cutting generic companies out of that market and keeping prices high for consumers.

industries.industry: Health insurers and government health programs
industries.note: Longer exclusivity raises drug spending for Medicare, Medicaid, employers, and insurers covering the affected drugs, costs that flow back to taxpayers and premium payers.
